If your mitogenomes were assembled elsewhere, for example by mapping to a reference
in Geneious, use `new_project_userAsmb()` instead. MitoPilot will skip assembly
and let you perform annotation, curation, and export.

The basics every project shares, what you need, how the mapping file is laid
out, and how a project is initialized, are covered in
[Starting Your Own Project](Your-Own-Project.html). Read that first if you have
not already; this page only covers what differs.

## Setting up the project

A user-assembly project needs one extra column in the mapping file, plus an
optional second:

| Column | Contents |
|---|---|
| `Assembly` | File name of the assembly FASTA for the sample (one file per sample) |
| `Topology` | Optional. `circular` or `linear`, for a single-contig assembly only |

`Topology` is your statement about a finished mitogenome you are handing over:
say `circular` and MitoPilot will not try to circularize it, say `linear` (or
leave the column out) and it may. It only applies to an assembly holding a
single contig. If the FASTA holds more than one contig, there is no single
answer to give, so MitoPilot records the sample as `multi`, ignores anything you
declared, and works out each contig's own topology as the pipeline runs. 

```r
new_project_userAsmb(
  path = "~/my_assemblies/run_01",
  mapping_fn = "~/my_assemblies/mapping.csv",
  data_path = "~/my_assemblies/raw_data",
  assembly_path = "~/my_assemblies/assemblies",
  executor = "local"
)
```

You still run the Assemble module, but it only maps reads to your assemblies to
compute coverage and error rates.

If you have no reads at all, set `no_raw_data = TRUE` and omit `data_path`.
MitoPilot will skip read mapping entirely and hide the coverage columns that
depend on it.

<div class="alert alert-warning">
<strong>Warning.</strong> A project holds either MitoPilot assemblies or
externally supplied ones, never both. Use separate projects if you have a mix.
</div>

## Finding the mitogenome in a whole assembly

If your FASTA files hold whole assemblies rather than mitogenomes, thousands or
even millions of contigs each, set `find_mitogenome = TRUE`. MitoPilot will
locate the mitochondrial contigs before anything else runs:

```r
# add to the new_project_userAsmb() call above:
  find_mitogenome = TRUE,
  mitofinder_db = "~/dbs/mitofinder_Percidae_refseq.gb",
```

MitoPilot BLASTs every contig against a bundled metazoan mitogenome database,
then confirms the best candidates by annotating them with MitoFinder. Only
confirmed contigs continue through the pipeline, as scaffolds of the sample's
assembly.

A nuclear scaffold carrying a mitochondrial insertion (a NUMT) matches only a
sliver of its own length, and is rejected on that basis. A sample carrying two
mitogenomes, its own and a contaminant's, yields both. A sample where nothing is
confirmed is marked failed with a note, and the rest of your samples carry on.

<div class="alert alert-warning">
<strong>Required.</strong> The confirmation step needs a MitoFinder GenBank
database for your clade. Build one with
`custom_assembly_db(clade = "<your clade>", db_type = "mitofinder")` and pass its
`.gb` file as `mitofinder_db`. Project creation refuses the search without it.
</div>

The **Mito Search** column of the Assemble table summarizes each sample. Click
the summary to open the full evidence: every contig considered, its length, the
reference it matched, percent identity, how much of the contig aligned, how many
mitochondrial genes it carried, and why it was kept or dropped. Thresholds
live in the **Find Mito Opts.** modal, and a per-sample log is written to
`out/<ID>/assemble/user/find_mito.log`.

On a real genome skim of 1.4 million contigs, the search returned the single
16,891 bp mitochondrial contig in about two minutes.

## Circularizing linear assemblies

Assemblers sometimes report a circular mitogenome as a linear contig whose end
repeats its start. Set `attempt_circularization = TRUE` and MitoPilot will try
to close linear contigs for you during the Assemble module:

```r
# add to the new_project_userAsmb() call above:
  attempt_circularization = TRUE,
```

Each eligible contig is compared against itself with BLAST. Every sample is
considered except those you declared `circular`, since you have already told
MitoPilot those are closed. A multi-contig assembly is eligible too, and each of
its contigs is attempted on its own. Click a sample's **Circularize Opts.** cell
to adjust the thresholds for circularization.

If the contig ends overlap, the duplicate end is trimmed and the sample is relabeled
`circular`. When you have raw reads, MitoPilot also maps them across the
new junction and leaves the assembly linear unless enough reads span it. This
mitigates the issue of repeats being mistaken for a real circle.

The outcome for every sample appears in the **Circularization** column of the
Assemble table:

| Note | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `circular: trimmed 231 bp overlap, 42 junction reads` | Closed, with read support |
| `circular: trimmed 231 bp overlap (no reads to confirm)` | Closed in a `no_raw_data` project |
| `linear: no self-overlap found` | The contig ends do not overlap |
| `linear: 231 bp overlap found but only 2 junction reads (5 required)` | Overlap present, reads did not back it up |
| `not attempted: 4,812 contigs exceeds max_contigs (100)` | Too big to work through contig by contig |

That last case only comes up on a whole draft assembly that reached this step
without a mitogenome search to narrow it down first. Turn on `find_mitogenome`
and circularization will see only the confirmed mitochondrial contigs.

Click the summary to see where the overlap sits, the two copies aligned base by
base, and the read depth across the seam. A sample whose overlap was found but
rejected shows the threshold it missed.

## Joining fragmented assemblies

Some assemblers leave the mitogenome split into more than one contig. 
Set `join_scaffolds = TRUE` and MitoPilot will order a sample's
contigs against its BLAST reference and join them into a single sequence
during the Assemble module:

```r
# add to the new_project_userAsmb() call above:
  join_scaffolds = TRUE,
```

A sample is eligible when it has a single assembler path made up of more than
one contig. If those contigs match different reference mitogenomes, MitoPilot
leaves them separate for review rather than joining them, so a contaminated
sample is never spliced into a chimera; the reason is left in the sample's
notes.

Because eligibility is any multi-contig assembly, not just mitochondrial
scaffolds, use `join_scaffolds` alongside `find_mitogenome = TRUE` on
whole-genome assemblies, so the join only sees contigs already confirmed
mitochondrial.

The joined result can be reviewed and adjusted by hand in the app, and
re-queued at any time with the **Redo Scaffold Join** button.
